variants.headline: Our new vassalage under {{master}}
body: At the muster yard, a clerk copies our names into {{master}}'s roll. The court keeps its seat, but those names can be called to their wars.

variants.headline: An era of our own counsel, concluded
body: So ends the account of the years our court answered in its own name. As of this entry we stand as vassals to {{master}}. The keeper of the record has put a ribbon at this page for the next person who has to find where it ended.

variants.headline: Tell us what protection we bought
body: We are now vassals of {{master}}, and their wars can become ours. The council should give its account of the bargain in the square. If our young people can be sent to fight for their towns, their families have a right to hear what protection there is for ours.

variants.headline: Our neighbors have a new court to bargain with
body: As a vassal of {{master}}, our nation loses the right to declare war on other powers. A neighbor with a dispute over a field or a fishing ground can now afford to hold out longer for terms. It depends how much interest the court of {{master}} takes in a quarrel over somebody else's land.

variants.headline: Our defensive pact with {{ally}} is over
body: On the frontier, the captain strikes {{ally}}'s countersign from the orders. The pact is over, both countries stay at peace, and each garrison keeps its road.

variants.headline: A defensive pact comes to an end
body: One of our defensive pacts has ended. We remain at peace with the other former signatory.

variants.headline: An attack on {{ally}} is their problem now
body: The defensive pact with {{ally}} has ended. The old planning maps in our staff rooms carried two sets of flags. A captain studying one of those maps today has to ask which posts his own garrison could hold if help never came.

variants.headline: Will you still send the next load?
body: Madam, on hearing that our pact with {{ally}} had ended, a driver asked whether I would still send her with the next load. I said I would. I have trusted the people who unload my wagons for twenty years, and I hope the two courts will give me cause to go on doing so.

variants.headline: We sign a defensive pact with {{ally}}
body: At the chancery, a clerk seals the copy for {{ally}} and gives it to a rider. The pact is signed. Whoever moves against one of us answers to both.

variants.headline: A defensive pact is signed
body: Our nation has signed a defensive pact with a major power. From this day, whoever moves against one of us answers to both.

variants.headline: Hear it! We stand with {{ally}}
body: Hear it, people of the nation! A defensive pact is signed with {{ally}}, and it holds from this day. A hand raised against either of us answers to both. Say it at your doors: an attack on {{ally}} is an attack on us!

variants.headline: A pact for the palace, a question for the street
body: The court has promised that if a hand is raised against {{ally}}, our banners march. Perhaps that is wisdom, and perhaps it is our sons who will make good on it. Read the terms aloud in the square before anyone cheers, and let the men who would march hear what they are marching for.

variants.headline: Letters from the court: a pact with {{ally}}
body: Letters from the court relate that a defensive pact has lately been concluded between our nation and {{ally}}. Two peoples who stand together in war are seldom asked to prove it, which all men of goodwill will welcome.

variants.headline: {{civilization}} denounces our nation
body: At the customs house, a tidewaiter reads {{civilization}}'s declaration to the traders in line. The denunciation is public, and the words sit on the record.

variants.headline: The square heard it first
body: A fishwife carried the news home from the market before any gazette had it: {{civilization}} has denounced us. By evening every stall in the square had an opinion, and most of them were loud.

variants.headline: Let the denunciation be answered
body: {{civilization}} has called our nation out before the world. Our answer is short: count the walls, count the friends, and give no apology that is not owed. Bowing to a shouting match is cheap today and dear every season after.

variants.headline: In this year, {{civilization}} spoke against us
body: In this year the court of {{civilization}} set down a denunciation against our nation, where none stood before. The scribe records the fact and the year, and sets down no opinion beside it.

variants.headline: First contact with {{stranger}}
body: Our people have met {{stranger}} for the first time. The two nations now know of each other, and neither is a rumor to the other any longer.

variants.headline: They say strangers came over the hill
body: It is told that our scouts stood a long while on the ridge, watching fires that were not ours. By morning they had a name for the smoke: {{stranger}}. The walkers came home with the story, and the story has not stopped traveling since.

variants.headline: A new people, and new roads to walk
body: Advices from the frontier bring word that our nation has opened relations with {{stranger}}. A first meeting is a door standing open: new goods, new charts, and one more chair at the table of nations.

variants.headline: We just met {{stranger}}
body: Confirmed: we have met {{stranger}}. They are on the map now. More as we learn it.

variants.headline: The mapmaker has a question about {{stranger}}
body: Sir, word of our first meeting with {{stranger}} has brought half the street into my shop. Each customer wants the name put at the end of a road he knows. If anyone who was there will show me where to put it, I can sell him a map at cost.

variants.headline: {{first}} and {{second}} sign a defensive pact
body: At the harbor office, the harbormaster has pinned the news beside the tide table: {{first}} and {{second}} have signed a defensive pact. A hand raised against either now answers to both.

variants.headline: Two foreign powers bind their defenses
body: A defensive pact has been concluded between two foreign powers. Neither signatory is ours, but an attack on either now draws the other in, and the neighbors of both are reading the change.

variants.headline: The pact between {{first}} and {{second}} redraws the arithmetic
body: In the war room, an officer has drawn {{first}}'s line and {{second}}'s in the same red pencil. Every staff that planned against one now plans against two. If the two hold to the letter, a war with either means a war with both. Alliances are cheap to sign and dear to test.

variants.headline: From abroad: {{first}} and {{second}} stand together
body: Letters from abroad relate that {{first}} and {{second}} have signed a defensive pact. A shipowner who calls at both countries' ports has asked her agents for news from both capitals before she loads the next cargo; a quarrel that starts in either can now reach the other.

variants.headline: {{first}} and {{second}} end their defensive pact
body: At the foreign office, an archivist has moved {{first}}'s file and {{second}}'s to separate shelves. The two remain at peace, but neither court can count on the other's troops if it is attacked.

variants.headline: A foreign pact falls away
body: A defensive pact between two foreign powers has ended. The two states are not at war with one another, and the change came quietly.

variants.headline: The quiet between {{first}} and {{second}}
body: The defensive pact between {{first}} and {{second}} has ended. Their neighbors used to reckon with the chance an attack would bring both armies into the field. A diplomat weighing the change now has two courts to sound out, and no promise joining their answers.

variants.headline: The fence between two gardens
body: Two neighbors took down their shared fence. The gardens still grow, and the fox is listening.

variants.headline: We declare friendship with {{friend}}
body: At the exchange, a wool broker has added {{friend}}'s name to the list of houses he will trust on a handshake. The friendship is declared in both courts, and the goodwill is on the record rather than in rumor.

variants.headline: A friendship declared
body: Our nation has declared friendship with a major power. The pledge is public, and the goodwill between the two courts is now on the record.

variants.headline: Hear it! Friendship with {{friend}}
body: Good news, good people! Friendship is declared with {{friend}}, and the word is official. Say it at your doors and say it twice: friendship with {{friend}}, declared and public!

variants.headline: Sir, a good word travels slowly
body: Sir, the news reached us late, as good news does: your nation and {{friend}} have declared friendship, and I write from the far side of that border to say it is welcome in our house. Two peoples who trade and talk rarely reach for blades. May this friendship pay its way in quiet years.

variants.headline: The tavern drank to {{friend}} last night
body: When the crier called the news, the whole room raised its cups to {{friend}} without being asked. Foreign policy is a long street away from here, but a friendly flag is good for business, and the landlord said so twice.

variants.headline: Our friendship with {{friend}} is over
body: At the customs house, a crate has come back from {{friend}} unopened, their seal still on the lid. The friendship is ended, and the two courts deal with each other now on plainer terms.

variants.headline: A friendship ends
body: A declaration of friendship between our nation and a major power has come to an end. The public goodwill it pledged is withdrawn.

variants.headline: In memoriam: the friendship with {{friend}}
body: It was declared with public words and toasted glasses, and for a season our two flags made a pleasant pair on the water. The declaration is ended now, and the friendship with it. What remains is the memory that such a thing was possible.

variants.headline: The end of the {{friend}} friendship, weighed
body: Declarations of friendship carry no armies, but they carry credit, and the court of {{friend}} has just withdrawn its account. What tends to follow is cooler letters and slower caravans before anything louder. At the exchange, a broker has already moved that court's paper to the back of the drawer.

variants.headline: Our court takes {{vassal}} as a vassal
body: {{vassal}} has become a vassal of our court. A merchant who supplies our garrisons says he has started asking what the roads are like between our towns and theirs.

variants.headline: {{vassal}} entered in the roll of vassals
body: In this season {{vassal}} came under the protection of our realm. Its court remained in its own seat, and in the rolls it was entered as our vassal.

variants.headline: A new source of tribute, a new frontier to defend
body: Our court can levy tribute from {{vassal}}. It has also taken on a frontier it may have to defend. In a quiet year the income could make the bargain look handsome. The test comes when a neighbor thinks it can have one of their towns before our troops arrive.

variants.headline: Let the magistrates of {{vassal}} set out what they can pay
body: Our court can set the tribute for {{vassal}}. Let the council hear from the magistrates there before it names a sum. They already collect the taxes and know what the districts can pay. By all means take the tribute; have the sense to take it at a rate that can be collected.

variants.headline: {{vassal}} is no longer our vassal
body: At the tribute office, the keeper of the ledger has closed the book for {{vassal}} and tied it with string. Neither court stands to the other as master or subject now, and what follows will be negotiated rather than commanded.

variants.headline: One vassalage ends
body: A vassalage binding another state to our nation has ended. Neither party stands to the other now as master or subject.

variants.headline: {{vassal}} walks free of us
body: Where our word once commanded, we now negotiate. At the border fort, the captain has been asked what ground he can hold alone; no answer has come. {{vassal}} walked free, and every other subject has noted it. The strong keep what they can hold, and our neighbors are asking what we can.

variants.headline: The vassalage of {{vassal}} comes to an end
body: The vassalage of {{vassal}} is at an end. One of the couriers who used to bring their accounts to our treasury tells us he means to come again on his own business. The innkeeper has promised him his usual room.

variants.headline: We and {{civilization}} denounce each other
body: {{civilization}} and our court have denounced each other in public. A merchant who keeps an agent abroad says he asked for both declarations before he sent out his next set of instructions.

variants.headline: Both courts put their quarrel on record
body: Our court and {{civilization}} have denounced each other in public. Their envoys can still talk in private, but it will be harder to disown a quarrel they have both committed to paper.

variants.headline: Two houses, one quarrel
body: When both neighbors shout at once, the market counts the broken pots. Quiet houses keep full shelves.

variants.headline: Who pays for the shouting?
body: Our court and {{civilization}} have denounced each other. In the foreign quarter, a cooper is wondering whether the customers who ordered his barrels will still come for them. Let the ministers tell the square what they're prepared to do if they don't.

variants.headline: We open our borders to {{civilization}}
body: At the frontier post, the toll keeper raises the barrier for a wagon from {{civilization}} without asking for papers. Our borders stand open, and their caravans may cross without leave.

variants.headline: Our borders stand open to a neighbor
body: Our nation has granted open borders to a neighboring power. Their travelers and caravans may now cross our land without asking leave at the frontier for each journey.

variants.headline: Notice to merchants: our roads are open to {{civilization}}
body: Take note, traders and caravan masters. Our borders stand open to {{civilization}}, and their goods and people may cross our land freely from this day. The frontier posts are instructed accordingly, and the toll houses will expect the traffic.

variants.headline: Open borders with {{civilization}}, and the goodwill they carry
body: An open border is a small treaty renewed each day by the people who use it. {{civilization}}'s caravans on our roads mean traffic at our markets and a neighbor with something to lose from trouble. A road that carries goods both ways is worth more than the guard posts it saves.

variants.headline: {{civilization}} opens its borders to us
body: At a {{civilization}} frontier post, our courier has ridden past without stopping for papers. Their land is open to us, and our caravans may cross without asking leave.

variants.headline: A neighbor opens its borders to us
body: A neighboring power has granted us open borders. Our travelers and caravans may now cross their land without asking leave at the frontier for each journey.

variants.headline: The road to {{capital}} is open
body: {{civilization}} has opened its borders to us, and our caravans can now reach {{capital}} without a permit at the frontier. Merchants who had priced that road for seasons were loading carts before the ink dried.

variants.headline: One wagon, loaded by noon
body: When word came down that {{civilization}} had opened the border, the carter on the east road had his wagon loaded by noon. "Stared at that road my whole life," he says. "First time it has gone somewhere."

variants.headline: {{from}} and {{to}} bargain, and a war ends
body: {{from}} and {{to}} have struck a bargain that requires peace with a third state. At the frontier, a carter who has been camped beside the barrier for a season is asking the guard when the road opens.

variants.headline: Peace is part of the price
body: A deal between two states has been recorded, and part of its price is peace elsewhere: one of the parties has agreed, in the bargain, to end a war with a state that never signed it.

variants.when: from !== null && to !== null && fromGives !== null && toGives !== null
variants.headline: The terms, as recorded
body: {{from}} gives: {{fromGives}}.
{{to}} gives: {{toGives}}.
The telling entry: a war, ended by signature instead of arms.

variants.when: from !== null && to !== null && ours === false
variants.headline: A war ends at someone else's table
body: The bargain between {{from}} and {{to}} includes peace with a third power. Someone at that frontier will be asking whether the troops can come home in time for the harvest. For the people still waiting, the next dispatch matters as much as the signatures.

variants.headline: War is written into the deal between {{from}} and {{to}}
body: A deal between {{from}} and {{to}} includes an agreement to make war on a third party. At the crossroads inn, a rider has changed horses and gone on with sealed orders. The landlord wipes the table and asks nothing.

variants.headline: A deal with war in the terms
body: A deal between two states has been recorded with war among its terms: one of the parties has agreed to take up arms against a state that had no say in the signing.

variants.when: from !== null && to !== null && ours === false
variants.headline: Tonight: a deal that buys a war
body: From the foreign desk tonight: {{from}} and {{to}} have signed a deal. Part of the terms is war on a third power. No shots reported yet. We are following this story and will bring you more.

variants.when: from !== null && to !== null && ours === false
variants.headline: Other people's wars, other people's coin
body: The deal between {{from}} and {{to}} puts a third nation's name on a contract it never signed. Our court had no seat at that table and no say in the terms. The question to put now, before the fighting finds our trade roads: what did we do while the ink dried?

variants.headline: Our vassalage to {{master}} is over
body: At the palace gate, a guard has taken down {{master}}'s pennant and folded it into a chest. The vassalage is ended, and our court's word is its last word again.

variants.headline: We are no longer a vassal
body: The vassalage that bound our nation to a foreign power has ended. Our state stands again on its own authority.

variants.headline: Hear it! We bow no more
body: Hear it, people of the nation! The vassalage to {{master}} is ended, and the word is official. Our court answers to no throne but our own. Say it in the square, say it at your doors, and say it twice!

variants.headline: In this year, the vassalage was dissolved
body: In this year the vassalage to {{master}} was dissolved, and the scribe sets it down as it stands. The tribute that came with it is paid no more; the protection that came with it is owed no longer. What follows is for the next hand to write.

variants.headline: Free, and with work to do
body: People, our word is ours again. If the council sends another envoy to {{master}}, let it read his instructions in the square. We have a right to hear what will be said in our name.

variants.headline: We denounce {{civilization}}
body: Our court has publicly denounced {{civilization}}. A correspondent waiting for a copy said other capitals would now have our words in full when they asked where we stood.

variants.headline: Said plainly, and none too soon
body: The denunciation of {{civilization}} is on the record, and plain speaking beats patient smiling. Words do not stop armies, but they tell our friends whose side we stand on while it still matters, and they tell {{civilization}} that the smiling is finished.

variants.byline: A reader who trades across that border
variants.headline: Sir, was there no quieter road?
body: I read that our court has denounced {{civilization}}, and I think of the carts that cross that border both ways each week. Quarrels are cheap to declare and dear to keep, and it is rarely the quarrellers who pay. If a word can be taken back with honor, I ask the court to weigh whether it should be.

variants.headline: In this year, we spoke against {{civilization}}
body: In this year the court set down a denunciation against {{civilization}}, where none stood before. The scribe notes the fact and the season; the judgment belongs to later hands.
